episode_title: Did Japan's "Last Ninja" Really Board Perry's Black Ships? Two Scraps of Paper, 1853
youtube_title: Did Japan's "Last Ninja" Really Board Perry's Black Ships? Two Scraps of Paper, 1853
youtube_description:
In July 1853, four foreign warships anchored off Uraga, and a man from Iga is said to have boarded one of them. The only trace is two sheets of paper kept by his family, and one account says the paper carries a watermark from 1856. Do two scraps of paper prove he boarded, or do they tell a different story?

📰 Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former Tokyo foreign correspondent. His grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to one day of Japan's past at a time. He can watch and he can speak, but he can never change what happens. Every episode is his dispatch from the scene.

🎌 Subscribe for new episodes 3 times a week:
https://www.youtube.com/@Samurai-Chronicles-JP

🌐 Official site: https://samurai-chronicles.com

🇯🇵 A Japanese perspective on Japanese history — created by a Japanese history enthusiast.

📚 References:
1. Iga-ryū Ninja Museum (Iga, Mie Prefecture) — Ninja Database entry on Sawamura Jinzaburo and the Sawamura family records
2. Hawks, Francis L. (comp.) — "Narrative of the Expedition of an American Squadron to the China Seas and Japan, Performed in the Years 1852, 1853, and 1854 under the Command of Commodore M. C. Perry" (1856)
3. Beasley, W. G. — "The Meiji Restoration" (Stanford University Press, 1972)
4. Turnbull, Stephen — "Ninja: Unmasking the Myth" (Frontline Books, 2017)
5. Waraku Web (Shogakukan) — feature article on the Iga ninja Sawamura Jinzaburo and his 1853 mission (2020; English edition 2025)

scenes.narration: I should explain. I am a correspondent, or I was, until my grandfather's brass watch passed to me. It carries me to any moment in Japan's past, for one day at a time. I may watch. I may speak. I may not change a thing. Today it sets me down on the shore at Uraga, at the mouth of Edo Bay, on the evening of July 8th, 1853. Out on the water sit four black American warships, two with paddle wheels, two sailing sloops. I have one day to learn whether a man from Iga ever climbed aboard.

scenes.narration: Let me give you the story first, the way everyone tells it. Japan's last ninja, Sawamura Jinzaburo, is sent to spy on the black ships. He climbs aboard in the dark, and comes home with bread, tobacco, candles and two sheets of paper. He is a hero of comics now, and a character in a video game. A word on Iga: it is the mountain country of central Japan where the ninja clans lived. It is a wonderful story. I came to find out how much of it is written down, and how much is only told.

scenes.narration: First, what is solid. The Sawamura were a family of Iga, and they served the Tsu domain, ruled by the Todo lords. They were not the shogun's Iga guards at Edo Castle; that is a different story. Their rank was musokunin: men with little or no stipend, but allowed a surname and a sword. One account says their duty was to light beacon fires. His name is Yasusuke. I cannot find the dates of his life, and I will not guess them.

scenes.narration: Who sent him? Two accounts, and they do not agree. One says the order came from the lord of Tsu, Todo Takayuki. The Iga museum says it came from the shogun's senior councillors. Both could be true, if the lord passed on a request from Edo. I cannot tell. The chief councillor then was Abe Masahiro, but I find no record that he named Sawamura. And on the water, I watch the American sailors wave the small guard boats away. Nobody is getting close to those ships tonight.

scenes.narration: Now the family's own papers. The museum names two documents the household kept. One is a record whose title means something like Notes on Secret Duties Performed. The other sets out the family's standing and descent. These are the family's words about itself, not an outsider's. I would give a great deal to read the first. I do not know whether the original survives or who holds it, and one reference work says the family papers were written down later. Until someone shows me, I treat it as the family's account of itself.

scenes.narration: Here is what the famous tale never tells me: how he got aboard. One summary of the family's papers says only that he came alongside a ship, and that the crew gave him the things he brought home. No rope, no disguise, no name of a ship. I stand at the water's edge with my notebook and I think the crossing is the whole story. The Americans keep boats away, I read. So a lone boat has a hard night ahead of it, and the story has a gap. I mark it.

scenes.narration: Later that night, a fisherman mending a net beside his beached boat told me, once I said I was a travelling merchant, that the foreign ships are as big as hills and smoke without any wind. He rowed out with the guard boats at dusk, and a foreign sailor waved him off. I asked about a man from Iga. He laughed. Nobody here asks where a man comes from tonight, he said, only what he saw. He went back to his net. I wrote down the laugh.

scenes.narration: Now I turn the pages of my notebook to the spring of 1854. Perry has come back, and on March 27th, during the treaty talks, he gives a banquet aboard his flagship for Japanese officials. One account says about sixty Japanese went aboard that day, and suggests that Sawamura may have been one of them. A Japanese reference work adds that the family papers set both of Perry's visits in 1853. If he was there, he did not creep aboard. He was invited, with a cup in his hand. But it is only an idea, and I have seen no list with his name.

scenes.narration: What do the Americans say? I read what I can find. Commodore Perry's own account of the expedition describes the banquet, the guests, the toasts. It does not mention a Japanese spy, or anyone creeping aboard, and I have found no sailor's diary that does. But I want to be fair to him. A servant, a bearer, an attendant: such men go unnamed in every navy's journals. Silence in the American record does not prove he stayed ashore. It only means the tale rests on Japanese paper alone.

I cannot tell you whose boat it is. This is where the story says he goes. I wish I could follow. But no record puts anyone on that deck, and I will not invent one. I stay on the stones and I listen. Then the oars stop, the mist closes over the water, and I am left with a question I cannot answer.

scenes.narration: Now the detail that unsettles me most. I turn to my notebook. One account says the two sheets of paper carry a watermark, and the year in it is 1856. If that is right, the paper was made after both of Perry's visits. 1853, 1854, then 1856: the year an American consul, Townsend Harris, reached Shimoda. So the paper may belong to a later meeting, or a later gift. I have only that one account, and I have not seen the watermark myself.

scenes.narration: What do the papers say? The museum calls them Dutch documents. Dutch was the Western language Japan's interpreters knew best, learned through the trading post at Dejima in Nagasaki, and Perry's men used it to talk to them. It is said that one sheet holds a crude sailors' joke about the women of three nations. The other holds a proverb close to still waters run deep. That is the whole secret. A man may have risked his life for a sailor's joke and a saying about quiet rivers. I do not know who translated them, or when.

scenes.narration: Who first read those papers, and when? I cannot find out, and I will not guess. Here is what I can say. A year before this night, I read, the Dutch had warned the shogunate's upper ranks that American ships were coming. Edo's officials were told, in translation, and the towns were not. I find no record that anything in Sawamura's papers changed a decision in Edo. I do not claim the two are linked. I only notice the contrast.

scenes.narration: Before dawn, I write my conclusion in pencil. Can I say he boarded? No. Can I say he did not? Also no. Here is what I can say. A family of Iga kept two papers. A family record says its man served in secret. And the black ships were here. The papers do not read like a break-in. They read like a brush with a world he could not read, and one summary of the family papers says the crew gave them to him. Perhaps he was handed them rather than took them. That is only my reading, and I mark it in my notebook as a guess.

scenes.narration: The watch grows warm against my ribs. My day is ending. One thing still troubles me. The papers were useless as secrets. A sailors' joke cannot defend a coast. Yet the family kept them for some 170 years, and the museum says they survive. Why? I think, perhaps, because they proved something other than a secret: that a man from a hill family once stood close enough to the new world to carry a piece of it home. I close my notebook. I look once more at the lanterns.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Back in my own century, I walk through Iga, in Mie Prefecture, where the ninja museum draws visitors from many countries. I read that the Sawamura house is not open to the public. I stand outside the museum and think how much of what I know about ninja came from stages, comics and games. The one trace of a real mission that survived on paper turns out to be a joke and a proverb. I think that is the most honest ninja story I have ever been told.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. The last ninja is a label, and I think labels are the least reliable part of any story. The museum calls him the last Iga ninja. A Japanese magazine says he is known as the last to do a ninja's secret work. I would put it more carefully: one of the last secret missions on record. Ninja were trained to leave nothing written down. This family left two scraps of paper and a record of its own service. Perhaps that is why we know him.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. In Japanese museums, a small word sits before the name on an object that is traditionally attributed to someone but cannot be proved. The word is den. It means handed down as. I have been thinking about den all day. A ninja handed down as the last. Papers handed down as proof. A ship handed down as boarded. I think it is an honest word, and one we could use more often, for what we love but cannot yet prove.

scenes.narration: That is all I can carry from the records: a family, two scraps of paper, and a ship nobody can place him on. The rest I leave open, because the rest is not written down. In my grandfather's notebook, the page in my own handwriting still reads only 1868. Subscribe, and the next dispatch will find you. The watch is ticking. Until the next report. Tokio Kamiya, reporting.
